content: 1. Shortened Tuberculosis Treatment in Adults: Studies have explored the efficacy of shorter treatment regimens for adults with non-cavitary tuberculosis who achieve culture conversion within two months. These regimens aim to reduce treatment duration while maintaining effectiveness. 2. Fixed-Dose Combination (FDC) Therapy: Research has compared the safety and efficacy of four-drug fixed-dose combination regimens versus separate drug formulations for treating pulmonary tuberculosis. FDCs simplify treatment and improve adherence but require further evaluation for bioavailability and effectiveness. 3. Tuberculosis Treatment in HIV-Infected Patients: Clinical trials have assessed the efficacy of six-month versus nine-month intermittent treatment regimens for tuberculosis in HIV-infected individuals. Shorter regimens may be effective, but patient-specific factors must be considered. 4. Management of Tuberculosis in Children: Guidelines recommend specific dosages of anti-tuberculosis medications for children, including isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. Treatment regimens vary based on disease severity, HIV status, and local drug resistance patterns. 5. Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis: Surveys and studies have highlighted the prevalence of drug-resistant tuberculosis in various regions, emphasizing the need for rapid molecular diagnostic tools and tailored treatment regimens to address multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). 6. Corticosteroid Use in Tuberculosis: Corticosteroids, such as dexamethasone or prednisolone, are recommended as adjunctive therapy for specific forms of tuberculosis, including tuberculous meningitis and pericarditis, to reduce inflammation and improve outcomes. 7. Shortened Regimens for Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis: Four-month regimens containing rifapentine, moxifloxacin, and pyrazinamide have been conditionally recommended for patients aged 12 years and older with drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis. For children with non-severe TB, a four-month regimen is also recommended. 8. HIV and Tuberculosis Co-Infection: Patients with TB and HIV should initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) within two weeks of starting TB treatment, regardless of CD4 count. This approach improves survival and reduces complications. 9. Treatment Adherence Interventions: Strategies to improve adherence to TB treatment include digital medication monitoring, material and psychological support for patients, and education for healthcare providers. Community-based treatment support is preferred over facility-based or unsupervised treatment. 10. Decentralized Care for MDR-TB: Ambulatory care models are recommended over hospitalization for managing MDR-TB, as they are more patient-centered and cost-effective. 11. WHO Guidelines on Tuberculosis: The World Health Organization (WHO) has consolidated guidelines for managing drug-susceptible and drug-resistant tuberculosis, emphasizing evidence-based recommendations for treatment regimens, monitoring, and care delivery. 12. Empirical Treatment for MDR-TB: In settings where rapid drug susceptibility testing is unavailable, empirical MDR-TB regimens may be initiated based on local resistance patterns and expert opinion. 13. National TB Control Programs: Countries are encouraged to use local drug resistance data to guide treatment policies and improve outcomes for patients with TB, particularly those at high risk of MDR-TB. 14. Pediatric Tuberculosis Treatment: Children with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or peripheral lymphadenitis can be treated with threeor four-drug regimens, depending on the prevalence of HIV and isoniazid resistance in the region. 15. Adjunctive Corticosteroid Therapy: For tuberculous meningitis, corticosteroids tapered over 6–8 weeks are strongly recommended. For tuberculous pericarditis, corticosteroids may be used based on clinical judgment and patient-specific factors. These findings and recommendations reflect ongoing efforts to optimize tuberculosis treatment, improve patient outcomes, and address challenges such as drug resistance and co-infections.
